1. The Inspiration: Adapting a Tournament Concept to the 82-Game NBA Grind
This project was sparked by an executive sports prediction dashboard that circulated on LinkedIn during the FIFA World Cup - combining match outcome classifiers, Monte Carlo bracket simulations, and a sleek Power BI analytics portal.
Adapting that concept to professional basketball, however, required engineering an entirely different architecture. Unlike a 64-match international soccer tournament with static four-year rosters, the NBA is an 82-game, 1,230-game endurance marathon characterized by rapid summer roster turnover, in-season blockbuster trades, back-to-back schedule fatigue, and multi-game playoff series where rotation depth dictates championship viability.

Throughout this project, one central question kept coming up:
How do real NBA front offices, Vegas sportsbooks, and elite media outlets (like ESPN or FiveThirtyEight) actually make these predictions?
Understanding that contrast gave us a deep appreciation for the trade-offs in sports analytics:

Player Impact
Proprietary spatial tracking metrics (Catch-and-Shoot QSQ, defensive contest distance, offensive rim gravity).

Roster Modeling
Lineup-level possession models tracking 5-man net ratings for hundreds of rotation combinations.
Top-9 rotation player aggregation—capturing over 90% of meaningful playing time during the regular season and playoffs.


Compute & Staff
Multi-million dollar cloud clusters and full departments of data engineers and quantitative analysts.
A modular, reproducible Python pipeline running in Jupyter notebooks on a single laptop.



Despite using public data, we discovered that grounding our features in basketball fundamentals—Dean Oliver’s Four Factors, pace-adjusted Net Rating, and Bayesian-shrunk player values—allowed our models to match the real-world predictive benchmarks achieved by commercial sports forecasting systems.

text:
3. The Big Engineering Challenges & Post-Mortems
Building this pipeline was not a straight line. Every phase revealed practical challenges that forced us to question our assumptions and design better solutions.


Challenge 1: The Rookie Dilemma (How do you value players with zero NBA minutes?)

The Problem: In standard machine learning pipelines, missing data is filled with zeroes. But if an incoming rookie has zero prior NBA games, giving them a value of 0.0 treats them as worse than an end-of-bench replacement player. This would severely penalize teams built around top draft picks (like Washington or San Antonio).
How Real Models Solve It: Sports analytics systems use college/overseas scouting numbers, athletic testing, or historical draft-position curves.
Our Solution: We looked at actual rookie-season production across recent NBA draft classes and established empirical draft-slot baselines:

Picks 1–3: Value of 6.60 (reflecting immediate high-impact starters like Cooper Flagg, Zaccharie Risacher, or Alex Sarr).
Picks 4–14 (Lottery): Value of 4.84 (solid rotation contributors).
Picks 15–30 (Late 1st Round): Value of 2.80 (bench contributors).
Round 2 & Undrafted: Value of 1.05 (developmental depth).
This gave incoming rookies a fair starting baseline without artificially inflating their teams.





Challenge 2: The Rotation Reality (Why 15-man rosters mislead)

The Problem: An NBA roster holds 15 full contracts plus two-way players. If you average the entire roster, a team with two superstars and four deep bench prospects looks average.
The Basketball Insight: In real NBA games, the 12th through 15th players almost never see the floor in competitive moments. In the playoffs, coaches shorten their rotations to 8 or 9 players. Starters and primary reserves play over 90% of the game’s total minutes.
Our Solution: We ranked every team’s roster by our workload-scaled Game Score and summed the Value Over Replacement Player (VORP) of only the top 9 rotation players. This accurately reflected real-game team strength.




Challenge 3: Why We Neutralized Home-Court Advantage in Future Simulations

The Question: In a single NBA game, home teams win roughly 58% of the time (+2.5 to +3.0 points). Why did we not include home-court advantage in our 2026-27 Monte Carlo simulation?
The Nuance: In single-game forecasting, home court is vital. But in an 82-game regular-season projection, every single team plays exactly 41 home games and 41 away games.
Over a full 82-game schedule, home-court advantages cancel each other out across the league. Adding asymmetric home boosts to future games can create calendar-order distortions. By using Bill James’ Log5 formula on a neutral scale, our simulation evaluates teams strictly on intrinsic roster strength and tactical efficiency.




Challenge 4: The Look-Ahead Leakage Trap (The 85% Accuracy Illusion)

The Trap: In early experimentation, our models achieved an eye-popping 85%+ accuracy predicting NBA games. It felt like a breakthrough—until we looked under the hood.
The Flaw: The model was using full-season averages and end-of-season win percentages. When predicting a game in November, the model was looking at stats that included games from March and April! It was reading tomorrow’s newspaper today.
The Fix: We completely eliminated full-season statistics from game prediction. We sorted all games chronologically and computed expanding rolling averages using strictly prior games (shift(1).expanding(min_periods=5)). On game day, Game N only knows what happened in Games 1 through N-1.
The Result: Accuracy dropped from an artificial 85% to an honest, realistic 67.0%. In sports data science, 67% out-of-sample accuracy on individual games is an excellent, production-grade result.




Challenge 5: The Superstar Flattening Trap & Empirical Bayesian Shrinkage

The Problem: Naive percentile rankings flatten talent. The gap between the #1 player in the world (Nikola Jokić) and the #15 player is massive, but percentile ranking treats it the same as the gap between #200 and #214. Furthermore, bench players who played only 3 games with hot shooting could post ridiculously high per-minute ratings.
The Solution: We implemented Empirical Bayesian Shrinkage: \[\text{Shrunk Value} = \frac{\text{GP} \times \text{Raw Value} + K \times \text{Replacement Level}}{\text{GP} + K}\] With shrinkage factor K = 8.0 games and an empirical replacement level of 3.90 (the median rating of NBA 10th-to-14th men), small-sample flukes were safely pulled back to earth, while superstars retained their massive, well-earned advantages.

text:
5. What Math Cannot See: The Human Reality of Basketball
As data scientists, it is essential to remain humble about the limits of numbers. No model, no matter how sophisticated, can foresee the unpredictable elements of an 82-game NBA season:

Catastrophic Injuries: A single rolled ankle or knee sprain in April can wipe out a 60-win team’s championship hopes in seconds.
The Trade Deadline Catalyst: In February, front offices make mid-season trades that completely overhaul rotations (e.g., acquiring a defensive anchor or a secondary scorer).
Locker Room Chemistry & Coaching Adjustments: Tactical counters, defensive matchups, and locker room trust cannot be measured purely through box scores.
Playoff Shooting Variance: In a 7-game series, an untimely shooting slump from 3-point range can knock out a statistically superior team.

Monte Carlo simulations do not claim to predict the future with 100% certainty—rather, they calculate the distribution of possibilities, allowing us to see which teams have the highest probability of weathering the storm.

title: Part 5: Project Conclusions & Reflections: The Journey of Building an NBA Predictor
text:
6. Final Reflections & Key Lessons Learned
Building this predictive pipeline from scratch provided invaluable practical lessons in applied sports analytics:

Look-Ahead Leakage is the #1 Trap in Time-Series Machine Learning:
Always ask: What was knowable at the exact moment before the event occurred? If you use post-game or end-of-season data, your model is not predicting—it is merely summarizing.
Domain Knowledge Beats Raw Complexity:
Standardized Logistic Regression with carefully engineered basketball features (Net Rating, Four Factors, Top-9 VORP) outperformed complex boosted tree ensembles. In basketball, knowing which numbers matter is far more valuable than throwing raw box scores into a black-box model.
Statistical Distribution Matters More than Raw Rank:
Standardizing player metrics into Z-scores and applying Bayesian shrinkage preserved the massive real-world advantage of superstars like Nikola Jokić, preventing them from being artificially compressed into simple percentiles.
End-to-End Pipeline Thinking:
From raw API extraction in Part 1 to clean feature engineering in Part 2, leak-free training in Part 3, Monte Carlo simulations in Part 4, and automated Power BI reporting tables in Part 5, sports data science is at its best when it tells a complete, coherent, and transparent story.

3. Game-Level Matchup & Per-Game Efficiency
Question: How do we calculate single-game shooting, turnover, rebounding, and Net Rating numbers for every matchup?
Each game produces two perspectives (one for each team). We pair both teams’ box scores side-by-side to measure offensive and defensive efficiency on every game night.

# building a small opponent side table (including OPP_PTS and OPP_DREB for ORB% and Net Rating)

    columns={
        'TEAM_ABBREVIATION': 'OPP_TEAM_ABBREVIATION',
        'WIN': 'OPP_WIN',
        'PTS': 'OPP_PTS',
        'DREB': 'OPP_DREB'
    }
)

# merging on GAME_ID to attach the opponent's stats to each row

    games_model_base,
    games_model_opp,
    on='GAME_ID',
    how='left'

# dropping rows where a team matched w/ itself

text:
4. Pre-Game Rolling Efficiency Features
Question: How do we measure team strength heading into a game without peeking at the game’s final result?
In real-life sports forecasting, you only know what happened before tip-off. For every game, we calculate an expanding average of each team’s prior games (shift(1).expanding()). Game N only sees how the team performed in Games 1 through N-1.


Code
# sorting chronologically within each season and team
games_model = games_model.sort_values(
    ['SEASON_LABEL', 'TEAM_ABBREVIATION', 'GAME_DATE', 'GAME_ID']
).reset_index(drop=True)

eff_cols = ['eFG%', 'TOV%', 'ORB%', 'FT Rate', 'NET_RATING']

# computing strictly pre-game expanding averages (requiring at least 5 prior games)
for col in eff_cols:
    games_model[col] = (
        games_model.groupby(['SEASON_LABEL', 'TEAM_ABBREVIATION'])[f'GAME_{col}']
        .transform(lambda s: s.shift(1).expanding(min_periods=5).mean())
    )

# building an OPP_ prefixed table of each opponent's pre-game rolling stats on that exact GAME_ID
opp_rolling = games_model[['GAME_ID', 'TEAM_ABBREVIATION'] + eff_cols].rename(
    columns={'TEAM_ABBREVIATION': 'OPP_TEAM_ABBREVIATION', **{c: f'OPP_{c}' for c in eff_cols}}
)

games_model = pd.merge(
    games_model,
    opp_rolling,
    on=['GAME_ID', 'OPP_TEAM_ABBREVIATION'],

This project delivers an end-to-end sports analytics, machine learning, and simulation pipeline that forecasts the regular season standings, postseason seedings, and championship outcomes for the 2026-27 NBA season.
Rather than relying on raw box scores or subjective power rankings, this prediction engine is built on an exhaustive nine-layer feature engineering architecture that translates player-level telemetry, contextual fatigue, and team efficiency into causal win probabilities:

Dean Oliver’s Four Factors: Quantifying the fundamental pillars of basketball efficiency for both offense and defense—Effective Field Goal Percentage (eFG%), Turnover Rate (TOV%), Offensive Rebounding Percentage (OREB%), and Free Throw Rate (FTR).
Pace-Adjusted Advanced Ratings: Normalizing scoring efficiency across differing game speeds to compute true Offensive Rating (ORTG), Defensive Rating (DRTG), and Net Rating (NET_RATING = ORTG - DRTG).
Causal Rolling Pre-Game Form: Calculating strictly backwards-looking 10-game rolling efficiency metrics and differential advantages (DIFF_ROLL_NET_RATING, DIFF_ROLL_EFG, etc.) knowable prior to tip-off, fully eliminating circular look-ahead data leakage.
Contextual Schedule Fatigue & Rest: Modeling rest days, back-to-back flags (B2B), and rest differentials (REST_DIFF = Home Rest - Away Rest) to capture physical fatigue.
Bayesian VORP Shrinkage: Applying empirical Bayes shrinkage (\(K = 8.0\), replacement level \(3.90\)) across multi-season player Value Over Replacement Player (VORP) metrics to stabilize small-sample variance while preserving generational superstar impact.
Rookie Draft-Slot Prior Imputation: Solving the historical “rookie valuation dilemma” by calibrating historical draft-slot priors (Top-3 Picks: 6.60, Lottery 4–14: 4.84, Non-Lottery 1st Round: 2.80, 2nd Round / Undrafted: 1.50) so high-impact rookies are neither ignored nor artificially zeroed out.
Rotation-Weighted Roster Aggregation: Filtering each 15-man roster down to the core top-9 rotation players by minutes and value (TOTAL_ROSTER_VALUE), capturing the postseason reality that bench depth matters far less than playoff rotation strength.
Playoff Experience & Resilience: Quantifying roster-wide cumulative career playoff games played (TOTAL_PLAYOFF_EXPERIENCE) to capture crunch-time poise and championship battle-testing.
Calibrated Modern Synergy Power Score: Unifying team strength through a balanced 40/50/10 formula: 40% historical franchise rolling efficiency, 50% Bayesian active rotation value, and 10% playoff pedigree.

These engineered features train a well-calibrated machine learning win classifier, which feeds into a 10,000-season Monte Carlo simulation engine simulating all 1,230 regular season games, the official NBA Play-In Tournament, and complete Best-of-7 playoff series to forecast the 2027 NBA Champion.

5. Dean Oliver’s Four Factors
Basketball games are won on four fundamental battlegrounds:

Shooting (eFG%): How well a team shoots, giving extra value to 3-pointers.
Turnovers (TOV%): How often a team gives away the ball per 100 plays.
Rebounding (ORB%): How often a team recovers its own missed shots.
Free Throws (FT Rate): How often a team draws fouls and gets to the line.



Code
# on games_regular_season, calculate each four factor at the game-row level first (per team, per game)

6. Pace-Adjusted Net Rating
Raw scoring totals can be misleading because fast teams have more possessions. Net Rating levels the playing field by calculating how many points a team outscores its opponent per 100 possessions.


Code
# estimating possessions per game (formula: FGA - OREB + TOV + 0.44 * FTA)
games_regular_season_merged['POSS'] = games_regular_season_merged['FGA'] - games_regular_season_merged['OREB'] + games_regular_season_merged['TOV'] + 0.44 * games_regular_season_merged['FTA']

# calculating per-game Net Rating (formula: (PTS - OPP_PTS) / POSS * 100)
games_regular_season_merged['NET_RATING'] = (games_regular_season_merged['PTS'] - games_regular_season_merged['OPP_PTS']) / games_regular_season_merged['POSS'] * 100

text:
8. Playoff Depth (Rounds Advanced)
Great regular-season teams do not always win in the playoffs. We track how far each franchise advanced in the postseason: First Round (1), Semifinals (2), Conference Finals (3), Finals (4), or Champion (5).


Code
# filtering games_combined to playoff games only
playoff_games = games_combined[games_combined['SEASON_TYPE_LABEL'] == 'Playoffs'].copy()

# creating a win column from the playoff_games
playoff_games['WIN'] = playoff_games['WL'].apply(lambda x: 1 if x == 'W' else 0)

# each team's opponent per game, using the matchup column
def get_opponent(row):
    teams_in_matchup = row['MATCHUP'].replace('@', 'vs.').split(' vs. ')
    teams_in_matchup = [t.strip() for t in teams_in_matchup]
    return [t for t in teams_in_matchup if t != row['TEAM_ABBREVIATION']][0]

playoff_games['OPPONENT'] = playoff_games.apply(get_opponent, axis=1)

# grouping by season_label and team abb to identify each distinct playoff series to order series chronologically and count wins within that series
series_summary = playoff_games.groupby(['SEASON_LABEL', 'TEAM_ABBREVIATION', 'OPPONENT']).agg(
    SERIES_START_DATE=('GAME_DATE', 'min'),
    SERIES_WIN=('WIN', 'sum'),
    SERIES_GAMES=('GAME_ID', 'count')
).reset_index()

# WON SERIES LOGIC
series_summary['WON_SERIES'] = series_summary['SERIES_WIN'] > (series_summary['SERIES_GAMES'] / 2)

# ranking series chronologically within each season
series_summary['ROUND_NUMBER'] = series_summary.groupby(['SEASON_LABEL', 'TEAM_ABBREVIATION'])['SERIES_START_DATE'].rank(method='first').astype(int)

# team-season furthest series (win or lose)
playoff_depth = series_summary.groupby(['SEASON_LABEL', 'TEAM_ABBREVIATION']).agg(
    PLAYOFF_ROUND_REACHED=('ROUND_NUMBER', 'max')
).reset_index()

# a team is champion if they reached the furthest round (4) and won that series
finals_results = series_summary[series_summary['ROUND_NUMBER'] == 4][['SEASON_LABEL', 'TEAM_ABBREVIATION', 'WON_SERIES']]
finals_results = finals_results.rename(columns={'WON_SERIES': 'WON_CHAMPIONSHIP'})

playoff_depth = pd.merge(
    playoff_depth, 
    finals_results, 
    on=['SEASON_LABEL', 'TEAM_ABBREVIATION'], 
    how='left'
)
playoff_depth['WON_CHAMPIONSHIP'] = playoff_depth['WON_CHAMPIONSHIP'].fillna(False)

10. Individual Player Valuation: Workload-Scaled Game Score
To measure how much each individual player contributes, we use John Hollinger’s Game Score (GmSc). Game Score blends scoring, shooting efficiency, rebounds, assists, steals, blocks, fouls, and turnovers into a single per-game rating.
We scale Game Score by playing time (AVG_MIN / 36.0) so that primary starters playing 34 minutes per game are credited appropriately, while bench players in limited minutes are kept in perspective.
To prevent small-sample distortions (for example, a player who looked great in only 3 games), we apply Bayesian shrinkage (K = 8.0 games) toward an empirical replacement level of 3.90. This pulls small-sample outliers toward a realistic baseline while letting proven stars keep their full rating.


Code
# pulling player-level regular season games for both seasons (cached in data/raw)
if PLAYER_REGULAR_CACHE_PATH.exists() and not REFRESH_API:
    player_games_combined = pd.read_csv(PLAYER_REGULAR_CACHE_PATH, dtype={'GAME_ID': str})
    print(f"Loaded cached regular-season player logs: {PLAYER_REGULAR_CACHE_PATH.name}")
else:
    player_games = []
    for season in ['2024-25', '2025-26']:
        gf = leaguegamefinder.LeagueGameFinder(
            season_nullable=season,
            season_type_nullable='Regular Season',
            player_or_team_abbreviation='P'
        )
        df = gf.get_data_frames()[0]
        df['SEASON_LABEL'] = season
        player_games.append(df)
        time.sleep(1)
    player_games_combined = pd.concat(player_games, ignore_index=True)
    PLAYER_REGULAR_CACHE_PATH.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    player_games_combined.to_csv(PLAYER_REGULAR_CACHE_PATH, index=False)

player_value = player_games_combined.groupby(['PLAYER_ID', 'PLAYER_NAME']).agg(
    GAMES_PLAYED=('GAME_ID', 'count'),
    AVG_MIN=('MIN', 'mean'), # Crucial for our minutes multiplier
    AVG_PTS=('PTS', 'mean'),
    AVG_FGM=('FGM', 'mean'),
    AVG_FGA=('FGA', 'mean'),
    AVG_FTM=('FTM', 'mean'),
    AVG_FTA=('FTA', 'mean'),
    AVG_OREB=('OREB', 'mean'),
    AVG_DREB=('DREB', 'mean'),
    AVG_AST=('AST', 'mean'),
    AVG_STL=('STL', 'mean'),
    AVG_BLK=('BLK', 'mean'),
    AVG_TOV=('TOV', 'mean'),
    AVG_PF=('PF', 'mean')
).reset_index()

# ---------------------------------------------------------
# Calculate John Hollinger's Game Score (GmSc)
# Formula penalizes inefficiency: missed shots, missed FTs, fouls, turnovers
# ---------------------------------------------------------
player_value['RAW_GmSc'] = (
    player_value['AVG_PTS'] + 
    (0.4 * player_value['AVG_FGM']) - 
    (0.7 * player_value['AVG_FGA']) - 
    (0.4 * (player_value['AVG_FTA'] - player_value['AVG_FTM'])) + 
    (0.7 * player_value['AVG_OREB']) + 
    (0.3 * player_value['AVG_DREB']) + 
    player_value['AVG_STL'] + 
    (0.7 * player_value['AVG_AST']) + 
    (0.7 * player_value['AVG_BLK']) - 
    (0.4 * player_value['AVG_PF']) - 
    player_value['AVG_TOV']
)

# ---------------------------------------------------------
# Apply Minutes Weighting
# Scales raw Game Score down if a player doesn't play starter minutes
# ---------------------------------------------------------
player_value['MINUTES_WEIGHT'] = player_value['AVG_MIN'] / 36.0
player_value['PLAYER_VALUE'] = player_value['RAW_GmSc'] * player_value['MINUTES_WEIGHT']

# ---------------------------------------------------------
# Empirical Bayesian Shrinkage (Regression to the Mean)
# Instead of hard-filtering < 20 games (which zeroes out injured stars),
# we apply shrinkage with K = 8.0 games (derived from split-half reliability r = 0.981)
# toward replacement level (REPLACEMENT_LEVEL = 3.90).
# ---------------------------------------------------------
K_PARAM = 8.0
REPLACEMENT_LEVEL = 3.90

player_value_clean = player_value.drop(columns=['PLAYER_NAME'])

roster_with_value_filtered = pd.merge(
    rosters_combined,
    player_value_clean,
    on='PLAYER_ID',
    how='left'
)

# Apply shrinkage to players with historical games
has_games = (roster_with_value_filtered['GAMES_PLAYED'] > 0) & (~roster_with_value_filtered['PLAYER_VALUE'].isna())
roster_with_value_filtered.loc[has_games, 'SHRUNK_VALUE'] = (
    roster_with_value_filtered.loc[has_games, 'GAMES_PLAYED'] * roster_with_value_filtered.loc[has_games, 'PLAYER_VALUE'] + K_PARAM * REPLACEMENT_LEVEL
) / (roster_with_value_filtered.loc[has_games, 'GAMES_PLAYED'] + K_PARAM)

# Display the top 15 highest valued individual players in the league
display(roster_with_value_filtered[has_games].sort_values('SHRUNK_VALUE', ascending=False)[['PLAYER', 'TeamID', 'GAMES_PLAYED', 'AVG_MIN', 'PLAYER_VALUE', 'SHRUNK_VALUE']].head(15))

11. Incoming Rookie Valuation: Draft-Slot Historical Baselines
Incoming rookies have never played an NBA regular season game, but assigning them a value of zero would be unfair to teams built around top draft picks.
Rather than guessing, we assign rookies an expected baseline value based on their draft position, derived from actual rookie-season production of recent draft classes:

Picks 1–3 (Top Franchise Talents): 6.60 (e.g. Cooper Flagg, Zaccharie Risacher, Alex Sarr)
Picks 4–14 (Lottery Picks): 4.84 (immediate rotation contributors)
Picks 15–30 (Late 1st Round): 2.80 (bench rotation prospects)
Round 2 & Undrafted: 1.05 (developmental depth)

7. The 10,000-Season Monte Carlo Engine
Question: How do we model regular-season variance, Play-In battles, and playoff series across thousands of possible outcomes?
Rather than locking playoff seeds in advance, every single simulation trial plays through the entire NBA calendar:

82-Game Regular Season (1,230 games): Intra-conference (52 games) and inter-conference (30 games) matchups resolved using Bill James’ Log5 formula.
NBA Play-In Tournament (Seeds 7–10): The 7-vs-8 winner takes the #7 seed; the loser faces the 9-vs-10 winner for the #8 seed.
Best-of-7 Playoff Brackets: Four rounds of seven-game series (First Round, Conference Semifinals, Conference Finals, and NBA Finals).

def build_nba_82_game_schedule(east_list, west_list):
    """Constructs a balanced 1,230-game NBA regular season (82 games per team)."""
    games = []
    # 52 intra-conference games per team (4 games vs 10 opponents, 3 games vs 4 opponents)
    for conf_list in (east_list, west_list):

        for i in range(n):
            for j in range(i + 1, n):

                num_games = 3 if dist in (1, 2) else 4
                for _ in range(num_games):

    # 30 inter-conference games per team (2 games vs each of the 15 opposite-conference teams)
    for e_team in east_list:
        for w_team in west_list:
            games.append((e_team, w_team))
            games.append((e_team, w_team))
    return games

power_map = dict(zip(projected_strength['TEAM_ABBREVIATION'], projected_strength['FINAL_POWER_SCORE']))
matchup_cache = {}

def get_matchup_prob(team_a_abbrev, team_b_abbrev):
    """Bill James' Log5 single-game win probability for Team A vs. Team B."""
    cache_key = (team_a_abbrev, team_b_abbrev)
    if cache_key in matchup_cache:
        return matchup_cache[cache_key]

    pa = power_map[team_a_abbrev]
    pb = power_map[team_b_abbrev]
    prob_a_wins = (pa * (1.0 - pb)) / ((pa * (1.0 - pb)) + (pb * (1.0 - pa)))

    matchup_cache[cache_key] = prob_a_wins
    return prob_a_wins

def simulate_play_in(top_10_teams, rng):
    """Simulates the NBA Play-In Tournament for seeds 7-10; returns final seeds 1-8."""
    s7, s8, s9, s10 = top_10_teams[6], top_10_teams[7], top_10_teams[8], top_10_teams[9]

    # 7v8 game: winner clinches #7 seed, loser plays for #8
    if rng.random() < get_matchup_prob(s7, s8):
        seed_7, loser_7v8 = s7, s8
    else:
        seed_7, loser_7v8 = s8, s7

    # 9v10 elimination game
    winner_9v10 = s9 if rng.random() < get_matchup_prob(s9, s10) else s10

    # Final Play-In game for #8 seed
    seed_8 = loser_7v8 if rng.random() < get_matchup_prob(loser_7v8, winner_9v10) else winner_9v10

    return top_10_teams[:6] + [seed_7, seed_8]

def simulate_series(prob_a_wins, rng, record_score=False):
    """Simulates a Best-of-7 series. Returns True if Team A reaches 4 wins first."""
    wins_a = 0
    wins_b = 0
    while wins_a < 4 and wins_b < 4:
        if rng.random() < prob_a_wins:
            wins_a += 1
        else:
            wins_b += 1
    if record_score:
        return wins_a == 4, wins_a, wins_b
    return wins_a == 4

def play_round(matchups, rng, record_list=None, stage_name=None, round_order=1):
    winners = []
    for team_a, team_b in matchups:
        prob = get_matchup_prob(team_a, team_b)
        if record_list is not None:
            a_won, w_a, w_b = simulate_series(prob, rng, record_score=True)
            winner = team_a if a_won else team_b
            record_list.append({
                'stage': stage_name,
                'round_order': round_order,
                'team_a': team_a,
                'team_b': team_b,
                'wins_a': w_a,
                'wins_b': w_b,
                'winner': winner,
                'series_score': f"{w_a}-{w_b}" if a_won else f"{w_b}-{w_a}"
            })
            winners.append(winner)
        else:
            winners.append(team_a if simulate_series(prob, rng) else team_b)
    return winners

8. Simulation Summary & Key Takeaways

Projected 2026-27 Championship Contenders (10,000 Seasons)

Denver Nuggets (DEN, 31.2% title probability): Led by Nikola Jokic’s league-leading individual VORP and elite historical Net Rating, Denver projects for 58.1 regular-season wins and enters the season as the overall championship favorite.
New York Knicks (NYK, 20.6% title probability): The top projected team in the Eastern Conference with 55.4 wins. Their veteran playoff experience (323 games) and balanced rotation give them a 38.4% chance to reach the NBA Finals.
Philadelphia 76ers (PHI, 14.4% title probability): High-end superstar talent carries Philadelphia to 53.5 projected wins and a 28.6% Finals appearance rate.
Oklahoma City Thunder (OKC, 12.2% title probability): An elite young roster and deep playoff experience (324 games) produce 53.9 projected wins. Their championship odds are tempered only by having to navigate a brutal Western Conference playoff path alongside Denver.
Second-Tier Contenders: San Antonio Spurs (4.8%, 50.0 wins), Houston Rockets (4.4%, 49.3 wins), and Cleveland Cavaliers (3.9%, 47.9 wins).



Key Analytical Takeaways

Conference Disparity & Path to the Finals: While Oklahoma City and Denver have comparable overall power scores to New York, the Western Conference playoff bracket is significantly deeper. New York reaches the Finals at a higher rate (38.4%) than OKC (22.3%) because the path through the Eastern Conference bracket presents fewer top-tier hurdles.
Play-In Tournament Drama: Simulating the full 7-to-10 Play-In Tournament captures realistic postseason bubble volatility. Teams like Minnesota (46.8W), Orlando (45.7W), Portland (44.9W), and Atlanta (43.2W) routinely flip playoff seeds through single-elimination Play-In games.
